title: Colony Call
short_description: Bats see with sound. In this family arcade adventure, every chirp lights up the dark caves for a moment, and every lost bat you rescue adds its echo to yours.
description: A rockfall has scattered the colony through the caves below the old forest. Two young bats, one for each player, are sent to bring everyone home. The caves are pitch black until you chirp, and each call outlines walls and creatures in glowing echoes before the darkness returns. Swoop through twisting tunnels, snap up moths for energy, and dart past spiders and owls that hunt by listening. Every call helps you see, but the hunters hear it too, so choose when to chirp and when to fly blind. Each cavern is a quick action run with lost bats to find; free them and they follow your flight path, adding their own echoes to light the way, so the bigger your colony grows the more of the cave you can see. Playing solo, your sibling bat follows your lead and echoes your calls; with a friend on the same screen, the two of you can split up, and two overlapping calls reveal far more than one. Simple top-down controls and gentle checkpoints make it a family game, while perfect runs reward score chasers. Gather every bat and lead the colony out at dusk.
pitch: A family couch co-op arcade game played almost blind: you see the caves only through echolocation, and every rescued bat adds its own echo, so the colony you rescue is also how you see.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Action, Family Friendly, Atmospheric, Top-Down, Arcade, Minimalist, plus Co-op and Split Screen modes) and parents with sound-reactive creatures pointed to a family arcade game built around sound. Probing showed 'a bat using echolocation to explore dark caves' sat far closer to the void than any of the scattered neighbours (zombies, corporate roguelike, launch sim).

title: Prime Time Planet
short_description: A pixel-art game show adventure about one stubborn mechanic trying to win back her family's farm on live television.
description: Welcome to Prime Time Planet, the most watched game show on television. Rook, a stubborn mechanic from a mining colony, signs up to win back her family's farm, and you guide her through every episode. On stage, every challenge is a small test of timing and nerve: cross collapsing bridges, dodge spotlights and answer the host's riddles before the buzzer. Between rounds you switch to the control room, a casual strategy screen where ratings become currency: buy sponsor gear, bribe the set designers, choose which hazards to face next and which rival contestants to sabotage. Backstage, you point and click through dressing rooms, prop stores and the editing suite to find tools, allies and secrets. The show is difficult and the hosts are cruel, yet the season follows a linear story with a beginning, a twist and a finale. Every episode Rook survives adds a little more to her kit and her fan club, so a run that starts fragile ends with a contestant the whole planet roots for. Can she survive twelve episodes, win the audience, save the farm and expose the network behind the cameras?
pitch: A linear, story-driven pixel adventure in which you are both the contestant on a cruel TV game show and her backstage schemer, spending ratings on sponsors and sabotage between short skill rounds.
interpretation: The decoded tags (2D pixel, casual, adventure, strategy, point & click, story rich, linear, female protagonist, incremental, difficult) and the heaviest parent (Pixel Gladiator's televised survival show) pointed to a broadcast-contest frame. Library, food-stall and photo-mystery takes scored far lower. The TV-show framing with a heroine and a strategy layer between stages was the only one that climbed.

title: Contraband Beard
short_description: Your beard grows while you sleep. Birds nest in it. It remembers everything. And in this kingdom, beards are illegal.
description: Grow the longest beard in the land, in a kingdom where beards are against the law. Royal barbers patrol every road, and a bare chin is the only safe chin. You are an old man whose beard has a mind of its own. Every night you sleep it grows a little longer, and it seems to be alive: sparrows nest in it, it stirs when danger is near, and it remembers the places it has brushed against. By day you wander villages, forests and castle towns, ducking into haystacks whenever a barber passes; by night you find somewhere safe to sleep. You explore, you hide, you sleep, and the beard grows. A longer beard is harder to hide, but it can lift, catch and remember things a shaven chin never could. Online, players can take the role of royal barbers and hunt each other's beards across the same countryside. Play it alone as a gentle, strange story about growing old in a kingdom that has forgotten its grandfathers, or online as a game of hide and seek.
pitch: A third-person stealth and exploration sim where your growing, living beard is your progression, your tool and the contraband you must hide, with an optional online mode where players act as royal barbers hunting it.
interpretation: The decoded tags call for a 3D third-person atmospheric exploration sim with a minor PvP strand. The odd parents and neighbours (mustache games, a masseuse sim, a tiny hero exploring a house) shared a theme of whimsical body care. Probing showed beard and barber premises scoring far above everything else, and adding the outlawed-beard and hide-from-barbers stealth twist gave the jump from 0.37 to 0.46.

title: Keeper of the Snowbound Keep
short_description: The siege is over and the snow is still falling. Clean up the aftermath, gather scattered arrows and lost belongings, patch the walls and get the castle ready for the next attack, alone or with friends.
description:
High in the mountains stands a realistic medieval castle, cut off by snow. All winter it held out against a siege, and now the enemy has gone, leaving broken carts, scattered arrows and frozen mud behind. Your grandfather was the castle's caretaker before you. Now the job is yours.

Work in first person through the realistic, snowbound keep. Shovel snow off the battlements, pull arrows from the gates, rebuild the walls stone by stone, and rescue the frightened horses, goats and chickens still hiding in the barn. Search the drifts for the belongings the villagers lost while sheltering inside, and sort the potions and spellbooks the old wizard left scattered across his study.

Then plan your season. Decide which repairs come first, where to store firewood and how to stock the cellar before the spring thaw opens the pass again, and whoever is waiting on the other side.

Play alone at a calm pace or bring up to three friends in online co-op to split the work. No combat and no blood, just the quiet satisfaction of turning a battered castle back into a home.
pitch: A nonviolent, realistic first-person co-op game set after a medieval siege: you don't fight the war, you clean up after it, searching for lost belongings, rescuing animals and rebuilding a snowbound castle.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Casual, Simulation, First-Person, Realistic, Co-op, Hidden Object, Family Friendly) and parents (wizard-tower organizing, a grave-relocation homecoming walk) point to a calm, realistic hands-on sim. Probing the direction showed it pushes hard away from space and sci-fi and toward medieval, snow, organizing and siege themes, so I read it as a cozy aftermath and cleanup sim in a castle.

title: The Last Updraft
short_description: Two estranged sisters, one last glider race across the ruined valley they grew up in. Play the story alone against your rival sibling, or split the screen with a friend and fight over every shortcut, memory and finish line in versus mode.
description:
Years after the war emptied the valley, the old glider race returns for one final season. Ada and June used to fly it together. Now they barely speak, and both of them have entered.

Every chapter is a head-to-head race between the sisters, part sport, part argument. You launch from broken towers, ride the wind through collapsed bridges and overgrown factories, and fight for the faster line. Between races, each sister explores the valley on foot, finds old letters and photographs, and solves small puzzles that open new routes: a shortcut their father built, a thermal above the dam where they once crashed.

In single-player you choose a sister and race the other, whose flying changes with what you learn about her. In versus mode, two players take a sister each in split-screen or online, and the story's ending depends on who wins the final course. A competitive sports game about family, rivalry and finally saying sorry.
pitch: A story-driven PvP sports game: the whole narrative is a head-to-head glider rivalry between two sisters, and when two players take a sister each, whoever wins the versus final decides how the story ends.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Action, Adventure, Puzzle, PvP, Racing, Sports, Post-apocalyptic) and the memory-driven parents and neighbours (ToMyX, The Squirrel & Sea, A Glider's Journey, When We Disappear) point to an emotional story told through a competitive sport. Score rose most when PvP versus play became the core of the story, not a side mode.

title: Beep Battle
short_description: A competitive metal detecting simulation for one to four players. Plan routes on a top-down tide map, then sweep a 3D beach in first person and dig for the best finds while drafting sneaky tools between rounds.
description: Beep Battle is a casual treasure-hunting simulation where friends and rivals compete on the same stretch of sand. Each round generates a fresh 3D beach hiding coins, lost rings, shipwreck relics, junk and the odd crab. Study the top-down tide map to plan your route, then drop into first person: sweep the coil, read the signal strength, and dig before someone else gets there. The water rises during the round, so anything you leave behind gets buried again. Between rounds, spend your haul in a roguelike shop and draft upgrades and tricks: wider coils, a pinpointer, decoy signals, sandcastles that block a rival's path, a seagull that steals someone's last find. After five rounds, the most valuable collection wins the beach. Play solo against cheeky computer rivals for a relaxed run, or invite friends online for loud, silly matches. Short sessions, bright visuals and simple controls make it an easy pick-up game for families and groups.
pitch: Metal detecting as a competitive roguelike party game: a top-down planning phase leads into a first-person dig on a shared beach, with tools drafted between rounds to outdig or sabotage your rivals.
interpretation: The decoded tags (3D, Casual, Simulation, Strategy, Top-Down, First-Person, Roguelike, plus some Multi-player/PvP) and the parent games (Metal Detector Simulator, Piratocon, Mexican Train, a survivors-like) point to a casual hobby sim turned into a strategic, multiplayer round-based game. A cozy reality-TV dig show landed on the existing 'The Dig Show', so I moved to competitive PvP rounds with a top-down plan and a first-person dig.

title: Wallcode 1920
short_description: In a frontier town in 1920, orders are written on walls. Paint codes for your squad, break the enemy's, and reach every checkpoint first.
description:
Wallcode 1920 is a realistic first-person war game where two teams paint the walls, break each other's codes and race to the checkpoints. Neither army trusts the radio, so orders are left in paint and chalk.

Every street is an arena. You carry a paint pot, a stick of chalk and a cipher notebook. Paint a symbol and your squad obeys it: wait, cross, breach. Enemy scouts paint their own, so you copy their marks, break the cipher in your notebook and paint over them to send their runners into a dead end. Hold every checkpoint before they do and the district is yours.

Between missions the story plays out as an illustrated visual novel in the signals office, where officers, couriers and a suspected traitor test your loyalty. Every run builds a new town with fresh ciphers; fall, and you begin again with what you learned and a new class unlocked: the runner, the codebreaker or the forger who can copy enemy handwriting.
pitch: A first-person war fought only through painted wall-codes: you guide your squad with symbols, crack and over-paint the enemy's chalk ciphers, and race their runners through the streets, with the story told as a visual novel between roguelite runs.
interpretation: The decoded tags are weak and scattered (first-person, strategy, realistic, visual novel, 2D/3D). The parents mix a 1920 war cipher game, a paint-the-map party game, a checkpoint-racing arena and a phone-operator visual novel. Probing showed the direction rewards genre mixes and penalises cozy or animal themes, so I combined cipher-breaking, wall-painting, checkpoint races and visual-novel interludes into one 1920 game.

title: Hollowfrost
short_description: Stranded on a frozen island with only a bow, a lantern and a talking owl, you explore a hand-drawn 2D map of glacier caves, solve ice-light puzzles and take aim yourself when the frost spirits wake each night.
description:
Your ship breaks apart in the pack ice and you wash up on Hollowfrost, an island that the maps refuse to show. All you carry is a hunting bow, a lantern and an owl who seems to know far more than she says.

By day you explore a hand-drawn 2D island as a side-scrolling platformer, cave by cave. Climb frozen waterfalls, leap between ice floes, and solve simple light puzzles hidden in old carvings: reflect your lantern off ice mirrors, melt the right pillar, line up the constellations on a stone door.

By night the frost spirits come, and the view drops into first person. Plant your feet, nock an arrow and aim for real, with a mouse or standing in VR. Fire arrows thaw bridges, rope arrows open shortcuts, and every spirit you calm drops a shard of warmth.

Spend those shards on new skills and gear, and use them to rebuild the old lighthouse at the island's peak. Light it, and a ship might finally see you.
pitch: A survival adventure that switches viewpoint every day: by day a hand-drawn 2D platformer for exploring and solving puzzles, by night a first-person archery shooter you can play standing up in VR.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Adventure, Action, 2D, Casual, Puzzle, Shooter, VR, FPS, 2D Platformer, Survival) pull in opposite directions. I read the void as one game that changes viewpoint: 2D exploration and puzzles on one side, aiming yourself in first person or VR on the other, which is the 'plan on the table, then take aim' idea from Tactical Archer, plus the hostile arctic survival of Link.

title: Pell's Long Winter
short_description: Play as a rat in an atmospheric 2D adventure where your choices matter and every night is a race against time. Bring food home before dawn and decide who you can trust.
description: Under the floorboards of a sleepy town, a rat family is counting the nights until spring. Each night you slip out as Pell, the eldest pup, with one job: bring food home before the sun comes up. Every outing is a tense little dash through the dark. Scurry between shadows, climb drainpipes and dart away from cats, owls and brooms. And every night asks something of you: share your find with the hungry mice next door, or keep it for your siblings? Take the safe road past the church, or risk the busy market for a bigger prize? Trust the sly crow who offers a shortcut, or the old sewer rat who never smiles? Each decision opens or closes paths through town, turns strangers into friends or rivals, and changes which of your family's stories plays out by the end of winter. Seasons turn the town around you: snow hides the trails, thaw floods the drains, and the people upstairs start setting traps. Gentle controls, soft hand-painted colors and no harsh failure make it welcoming for younger players, while many endings reward anyone who wants to see every path.
pitch: A family-friendly, choices-matter story told through short timed foraging runs: each night is an arcade dash against the dawn, and what you do with the food decides your rat family's winter and its ending.
interpretation: The void decodes as Atmospheric, 2D, Casual, Action and Choices Matter with a single-player focus, and its parents mix racing, maze and arcade games. Probes put 'play as a rat … choices matter … every night is a race against time' far above the racing, maze and courier ideas I tried.

title: Out the Door
short_description: Fight the fluffy anxiety monsters that stop a shy girl from leaving her apartment, one cute, colorful action roguelike run at a time.
description: Juniper has not left her tiny apartment in weeks. Every time she reaches for the door, her worries come out to play as round, fluffy monsters. In this cute 3D action game you help her push back. Every outing is a short run through her neighborhood, and every day the worries take new shapes. Dodge soft, colorful bullet patterns, bonk monsters with a pillow, a houseplant or a trusty umbrella, and collect small courage charms that change how you fight. When a run ends, nothing is lost. Back home, a relaxing life sim lets you water plants, cook a simple meal, text a friend or tidy up, and each calm moment unlocks new abilities for tomorrow. Grow braver every day until the front door is just a door again.
pitch: A cute, gentle 3D bullet-hell roguelike about social anxiety: each run takes a shy girl a little farther from her front door, and calm life-sim time at home powers up the next outing.
interpretation: Decoded casual + action + cute + 3D + action roguelike + relaxing + simulation, plus psychological and social-anxiety parents and neighbours (JNZ, Monster Networking), pointed to a cute action game about inner struggles. Hedgehog postman, supermarket and island-farm takes stayed near 0.16-0.24. Pairing a cute bullet hell with a life sim about anxiety is what reached the void.

title: Wren and Clover
short_description: A young noble girl and her little tank must prepare their tiny country for war. Recruit knights, archers and cooks, and get everyone ready in time.
description: Her name is Wren. Her tank is called Clover. Clover has never fired a shot; her grandfather swapped the cannon for a watering can. Roll across flower meadows, snowy passes and sandy beaches. Repair bridges, clear roads and rebuild windmills. Visit castles, farms and fishing villages, recruit knights, archers and cooks, and practise archery and horse riding with the old general. Every friend you make joins the cause with a skill of their own, and every upgrade makes Clover faster, stronger and a little bit cuter. Explore a big open countryside at your own speed and enjoy the beautiful scenery. No stress, no timers, just fun. Supports VR headsets and gamepads, and can also be played on a flat screen with a mouse and keyboard. When summer ends, all your preparation, and all the friends you made on both sides of the border, decide whether the war happens at all.
pitch: A cozy, no-combat 3D adventure RPG, playable in VR, where a noble girl and her repurposed tank get a tiny kingdom ready for a war through exploring, repairing and making friends, and may stop it from happening at all.
interpretation: Very casual, cute and relaxing fantasy with a female lead and VR, mixed with military and vehicle signals from the parents (the noble girl on the brink of war in Paths Taken, the Mars rover exploring and upgrading, a military strategy game). The top single-tag probes were Tanks, Military and Tabletop, and the anti-horror direction was strong, so I read it as a wholesome war-preparation road trip with a harmless tank.

title: A Long Bounce Home
short_description: Play as a squishy alien slime with a tiny bow, stranded in a colorful forest after a meteorite crash. Bounce, stretch and shoot glowing arrows through bright glades and dark underground caves to collect the fragments you need to fly home.
description:
A meteorite has crashed into a strange, colorful forest on Earth. Riding inside was Blip, a small alien slime with a tiny bow, and its little ship is now a hundred glowing fragments scattered across glades, rivers and deep caves.

Play in third person as a squishy alien slime with a tiny bow. Bounce off mushrooms, stretch across gaps, roll down hills and stick to walls with physics-driven movement that feels great to master. Forest critters do not appreciate visitors, so fire glowing arrows to pop beetles, scare off owls and light up the dark underground caves where the biggest fragments landed.

Every trip underground is different. Tunnels shift, new creatures appear and power-ups like split arrows, double bounce or a sticky shell change how each run plays. Bring fragments back to the crash site to rebuild your ship piece by piece and unlock new hats, colors and abilities for your slime.

Short, colorful arcade runs, gentle atmosphere and a cute hero make it easy to pick up, while hidden paths and tricky bosses reward players who want to explore every corner.
pitch: A casual 3D action roguelike starring a stretchy physics slime that fights with a bow: bouncy movement and glowing arrows that light up procedurally shifting caves, in place of the usual top-down twin-stick shooting.
interpretation: The void reads as Action, Casual, Arcade, Colorful, Action Roguelike, Third Person and Physics, and it points sharply away from anything strategic or turn-based. A parent is a creature that lands on Earth inside a meteorite. Probes favored archery, an alien slime, a colorful forest and underground caves, which add up to a cute, physics-driven archery roguelite.

title: Ashgrove After Dark
short_description: Run a small shelter for strange creatures at the edge of an empty town that rearranges itself every night. Explore its streets in first person, take in what you find, and send your creatures into turn-based battles against the things that follow you back.
description:
The shelter on Ashgrove Lane was cheap for a reason. The town beyond the gate has been empty for years, and every night its streets, shops and apartments quietly swap places. The creatures that wander out of it are not in any book.

By day you run the shelter: cook feed, build pens, clean, heal and befriend residents like the lantern-cat, the paper fox and the slow, enormous moss-hound. By dusk you walk into town with a flashlight, mapping streets that will be gone tomorrow, solving small puzzles to open locked buildings, and searching for new creatures. Other keepers can join your town online to explore with you, or face your creatures in turn-based PvP duels.

Some things in the town do not want to be found. When they catch up with you, your creatures fight in turn-based battles where trust, mood and the light you carry matter as much as strength. A cozy management sim slowly turning into something stranger.
pitch: A cozy creature-shelter management sim joined to first-person exploration of a town that rebuilds itself every night, where the creatures you care for fight in turn-based battles that depend on their trust and mood, against the town's horrors or against other keepers online.
interpretation: The parents mix creature care (Dragon Shelter, Familiars.io), a creeping board-game corruption (The Encroaching) and apartment horror (Dead Stop - The Tenant), and the decoded tags are Exploration, Simulation, Casual, Strategy, PvP, Turn-Based Combat and Psychological Horror. I read this as a cozy creature sim that slowly turns into horror. An urban setting scored better than a forest one, and so did a PvP mention placed early in the text.

title: Lantern Isles
short_description: Explore a chain of cute islands, find what the last settlers hid, and grow tiny villages that defend themselves at night. A casual mix of point-and-click searching, small real-time battles and bullet hell shooting from the lighthouse.
description: Lantern Isles is a casual 2D strategy adventure across a handful of small islands. You arrive by boat with a few villagers and a lantern. On each island, point and click through illustrated scenes to search for hidden tools, seeds and old maps left behind by the settlers who came before. Every item you find unlocks something: a sawmill, a watchtower, a new villager with a special skill. Assign villagers to gather, build and farm in real time, and expand your settlement across the island. At night, mischievous sea spirits come ashore in glowing swarms. Command your villagers to hold the walls, then take the lighthouse cannon yourself and weave its beam through bullet hell patterns to shoot down the brightest spirits. Each island has a small puzzle at its heart and a keeper who levels up your crew with new abilities. Sessions are short, the art is soft and colorful, and the challenge grows gently as you sail from one island to the next.
pitch: Hidden-object searching powers a cute 2D real-time village builder, and each night ends in a bullet hell defence that you fly yourself from the lighthouse.
interpretation: The void mixes casual 2D strategy (cute RTS like Feyght) with point & click hidden-object adventure and a shooter/bullet hell strand (D'LIRIUM), with an island-survival parent (ToGather:Island). The island setting plus a bullet hell night phase gave the biggest jumps; bakery and toy-soldier versions stalled around 0.24.

title: Spike of Peace
short_description: No more battles. The elves and dwarves will settle their war with volleyball. Dive, spike and survive spell-filled rallies as a young elf who never wanted to fight.
description:
Spike of Peace is a colourful third-person physics volleyball game, cute on the surface, difficult in the hands and emotional at heart. For a hundred years elves and dwarves fought over the valley; now every border is decided by a match on the sand.

You play as Lirra, a young elf who lost her brother in the last battle and now captains a village team nobody believes in. The campaign is an action roguelike road trip: each run brings random rivals, courts and blessings that change how the ball flies. Lose a match and the road starts again, but your friends grow closer every time.

Rallies are physics-driven and difficult. You control every jump, dive and spike, and dwarf teams hurl enchanted serves that burst into storms of bouncing orbs, so each point becomes a small bullet hell you survive with timing and nerve.

Between matches, quiet story scenes deal with friendship, old grudges and what peace really costs. Play solo, or bring a friend for split-screen two-on-two.
pitch: A fantasy war replaced by a volleyball tournament: hard, physics-driven 3D rallies where enemy spells turn each point into a small bullet hell, built as an emotional action-roguelike road trip with split-screen 2v2.
interpretation: The decoded tags point to cute, colourful, difficult 3D third-person physics action with roguelike, bullet-hell, sports and emotional elements, plus split-screen modes. Single-tag probes favoured Elves, Volleyball, War and Emotional, and pushed away from mystery and detective themes. So the game is a heartfelt fantasy-war story played out as volleyball.

title: Camp Larkhollow
short_description: A casual point-and-click camp simulation by day, a top-down shoot 'em up by night. Run a fantasy summer camp for young wizards, grow it with incremental upgrades, level up your counselors, and grab a wand after dark to blast mischief spirits away.
description:
Every summer, families from across the kingdom send their children to Camp Larkhollow to learn a little magic and a lot about each other. This year, you are the new camp director.

Days are for planning. From a top-down view of the camp, point and click to schedule lessons, assign counselors, stock the kitchen and decide who goes canoeing. A good plan keeps campers happy; a bad one ends with a frog outbreak in the dining hall.

Evenings are for stories. Sit by the campfire, talk with campers and staff, and help a shy kid find her spell or settle a rivalry between cabins.

Nights are for defense. Mischief spirits drift out of the forest, and the game becomes a light top-down shoot 'em up: grab your wand, sweep the paths and blast glowing swarms back into the trees before they reach the cabins.

Every calm night earns camp points that feed a gentle incremental climb: new activities, bigger cabins, better wands and level-ups for your counselors. By summer's end, Larkhollow should be the happiest camp in the realm.
pitch: A camp-management sim where each day has three parts: point-and-click scheduling, campfire stories and a top-down wand shoot 'em up at night, all feeding one incremental upgrade loop.
interpretation: The void is a casual mix of Simulation, Strategy, Top-Down Shooter, Shoot 'Em Up, Incremental and Point & Click, with a light Fantasy/RPG layer. Its parents mix horde defense (Heavenly Battle, Melon Simulator) with a memory-camp visual novel (My Camp of Memories), so I built a calm management sim with a horde-defense phase at night. Fantasy proved essential: the same design set at a non-magic camp collapsed to 0.08.

title: Wallnut Winter
short_description: A surreal first-person action puzzle game about rodents racing through a snowed-in house that turns abstract after dark. Play as a mouse, a squirrel, a beaver or a hamster, alone, in co-op or head to head.
description: Snow has buried the old house on the hill, and the four rodents sheltering in its walls, from the house mouse to a beaver who wandered in from the frozen pond, are cut off from their winter stores. After dark the house turns surreal: rooms float apart, stairs fold over and the snow falls upward. Each rodent has its own talent. The mouse squeezes through tiny gaps, the squirrel climbs and leaps, the beaver gnaws and builds bridges, and the hamster rolls in its ball to power old machines. Puzzles mix all four: chew a beam into a ramp, roll the hamster across it, then send the mouse through the gap it reveals. Every room is also a race against the dawn, because the house snaps back to normal at sunrise and anything left behind is lost. Play the story alone and switch between the four at any time, or invite up to three friends to each take a rodent in online or local co-op. Once a room is solved, unlock it in race mode and see who can reach the exit first. Gather the stores and find out what keeps the house dreaming.
pitch: A first-person, rodent's-eye co-op puzzle game where four species with different abilities solve a snowbound house that becomes abstract each night, and every solved room turns into a head-to-head race.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Action, Puzzle, Family Friendly, Atmospheric, First-Person, Surreal, Abstract, Co-op) plus a rodent puzzle parent and snowy-house and music-racing neighbours suggested a surreal family co-op puzzle game. Probes showed 'rodents', a snowy house and racing each pushed the score up.

title: Multiverse Cup
short_description: Race through a different universe every lap, shooting rivals and adapting to new physics. One life per cup, no second chances.
description: Welcome to the Multiverse Cup, the only race where the track changes reality under you. Each lap jumps the whole field into a different universe: low gravity, flipped upside down, made of candy, on fire, or drowned under a purple ocean. Your blaster matters as much as your engine: shoot rivals, clear debris and open shortcuts between worlds. The single-player campaign is a roguelike adventure: your racer has one life per cup, damage carries over between laps, and every universe you survive offers a new part, weapon or perk to bolt onto your hovercraft. Lose your racer and the next one starts from scratch. Switch between a third-person chase camera and a first-person cockpit at any time. In online PvP up to eight pilots race head to head, or team up with a friend in online co-op to run the campaign together. Learn the rules of each world, find the shortcuts between dimensions and become the champion of every reality.
pitch: A permadeath roguelike combat racer where every lap shifts the whole field into a different universe with its own physics, so you have to adapt, shoot and keep one fragile hovercraft alive.
interpretation: The parents mix a universe-shifting platformer (Verse Jumper), kart racing (Moorhuhn Kart 2) and shooter/roguelike games, and the decoded tags add racing, PvP, perma death, sci-fi and both camera views. Jetpack, kart and sci-fi biathlon takes reached 0.14-0.27. Racing through a new universe each lap, with permadeath cups and online PvP or co-op, jumped to about 0.48 and was refined from there.

title: Dumplings After Dark
short_description: The city fell to the dead, and the gangs now run what is left. Keep your dumpling bar open, pay for protection, and feed the survivors.
description: Mio inherited the dumpling bar from her grandfather the week the city fell. Now the dead wander the streets, the Kurose gang controls the harbour and the night market, and rival gangs fight over the blocks around her shop. Every week the gang comes to collect, and every week you find a way to pay. By night you sneak through the ruined city in top-down 2D, scavenging flour, cabbage and gas canisters, and fighting off the infected with kitchen knives, frying pans and anything else you can find. By day you open the doors, cook for the survivors and trade dumplings for bullets, medicine and information. Regulars come back day after day, each with a story to tell and a skill to offer. Unlock new recipes, upgrade your kitchen and expand the bar. A second player can join in local co-op as the bar's bodyguard. Several endings depend on which gang you side with, and on whether you can keep the last restaurant in the city open.
pitch: A top-down 2D anime restaurant-management and survival game in which you run the last dumpling bar in a zombie-overrun city held by rival gangs: scavenge by night, cook and trade by day, and pay protection to survive.
interpretation: The parents mix zombie survival RPG (XZ), a sushi-building roguelike, an anime rural-town adventure and a railway business sim. The decoded tags read as 2D, story-rich, top-down anime with crafting, survival and co-op, and tag probes leaned to crime and business. Food business plus gang debt plus zombie apocalypse scored best. Switching sushi to dumplings raised both target_sim and novelty, because several sushi games already exist.

title: Rocky Road Rampage
short_description: A small seaside town is overrun by zombies in the middle of summer. Drive your ice cream truck through the outbreak, ram zombies, serve survivors and upgrade your van while your little robot sidekick shoots from the roof.
description:
Sunny Shores was the perfect summer beach town until the zombies arrived. Now everyone is hiding indoors, and the only vehicle still on the road is yours: a cute, battered ice cream truck driven by a retired soldier who just wanted a quiet life.

Drive through a bright, cartoony 3D town in a casual action simulation. Follow the jingle to hungry survivors, park, and serve cones and popsicles before the music draws a crowd. Then floor it. Ram zombies with your truck, swerve through alleys and let your little robot sidekick, riding on the roof, blast anything that gets too close.

Every sale earns cash and experience. Spend it on armor, bigger freezers, monster-truck tires and silly weapons like the sprinkle cannon, and level up your driver and robot. Clear each neighborhood's boss to open new roads along the coast.

No gore, just goofy zombies, sticky fingers and the satisfying chaos of running a business at the end of the world.
pitch: A vending simulation and a vehicular action RPG in one loop: every sale of ice cream rings the jingle that draws the horde, so running the business and surviving the outbreak are the same activity.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Action, Simulation, Casual, 3D, with traces of RPG and Action RPG) point to an action sim, and the direction is strongly anti-puzzle and anti-mystery. The parents mix an ice cream truck sim, a platformer with a mecha ally, a soldier FPS and a restaurant idler, and probes favored driving, zombies and truck action. That gave a soldier and his robot sidekick running an ice cream truck through a zombie outbreak.

title: The Lantern Cats
short_description: Keep a little lantern burning for a family of sleepy cats. Nudge floating islands into orbit around its light, decide which islands stay warm and which drift into the dark, and watch the tiny lives on them change with every choice.
description:
At the bottom of an endless night hangs one small lantern, and you are its keeper. Floating islands drift in from the dark, and with a gentle push you can pull them into orbit around the light, where meadows, villages and strange gardens begin to grow.

Everything moves with soft, real physics, so every island you add tugs on all the others. Sessions are short and calm, with a little action: flick away falling embers, catch drifting rocks before they collide, spin a little moon, string bridges of light between neighbours. Then the cats ask for something. Bring one island closer to the flame and another freezes in shadow. Let two peoples meet, or keep them apart. Feed the lantern, or let it dim.

Your choices ripple through the whole sky, and no two finished worlds look the same. Cute, colourful and quietly melancholy: a relaxing simulation about caring for something much larger than you.
pitch: A relaxing 2D orbital-physics caretaking sim where every island you place pulls on the others, and the choices about who gets the lantern's limited light branch the story toward many endings.
interpretation: The decoded tags (Casual, 2D, Choices Matter, Simulation, Relaxing, Cute, Physics, a touch of dark fantasy) and the parents (Orbitous gravity, Nothing But Cats, the choice-heavy Flawless Abbey) suggest a gentle physics sim with real moral choices. Gravity caretaking scored best. Adding cats lifted the score further without the low novelty of a desktop-pet version.

title: Night Choir
short_description: Ride a motorbike through the dreams of a sleeping town. Race along roads built by music, fight off the riders of its nightmares, and piece together the story of the night everyone stopped waking up.
description: Night Choir is a third-person racing adventure set inside dreams. One night every resident of a small coastal town fell asleep and never woke. You arrive on an old motorbike and discover you can ride into their dreams, where roads are built from the music each sleeper remembers. Race along winding melodies over oceans, through ruined cathedrals and across endless rooftops, keeping your speed in time with the song to stop the road from collapsing. In the darker dreams, shadow riders hunt you down, and you fight back at full speed, shoving them off the road and breaking their chains before they reach the dreamer. Off the bike, explore each dream on foot, talk to the dreamers and find the memories that explain why they cannot wake. Each rescued sleeper adds a new instrument to your bike's radio and opens new roads. The whole journey can be played on a flat screen or in VR, and a split-screen mode lets two friends race the finished dream roads head to head. Atmospheric, musical and story-rich, it is a racing game you play for the journey.
pitch: A story-driven racing adventure where the tracks are built from music inside sleepers' dreams. You keep in time with the song so the road holds, fight nightmare riders at speed, and explore on foot to wake the town.
interpretation: The decoded tags read as a story-rich, atmospheric 3D third-person adventure with an odd Racing signal and some split-screen PvP. Its parents mix a musical VR relaxation space (SZEN), a brutal fantasy sport and medieval RPGs. Medieval racing versions scored ~0.23; adding SZEN's music and dreamlike side to a racing adventure, with combat and split-screen, scored best. I left out the adult tags that the void's decoder also reads.

title: Sprue Arena
short_description: Snap together a dinosaur model kit, paint it, then drop it onto the table and blast waves of wind-up invaders in casual top-down co-op.
description:
Sprue Arena is a casual 3D action game in two halves: a relaxing hobby workbench and a fast top-down battle table.

At the bench you snap parts from plastic runners and plan your build like a strategy puzzle with a limited budget of parts. Mix a raptor frame with a triceratops shield head and a rocket tail, paint your mechanical dinosaur, and test it on the cutting mat.

Then you drop it onto the table. Desks, shelves and living room floors become PvE battlefields where waves of wind-up invaders pour out of toy boxes. Stomp, dodge and shoot in arcade top-down combat, grab spare parts to repair mid-fight, and clear the wave to unlock new kits.

Play solo or bring up to three friends in online co-op, each with their own build. Combine roles, revive teammates and chase high scores on daily tables. Short rounds, deep customisation and no pressure between battles make it easy to pick up for one more build.
pitch: A relaxing model-kit hobby sim and an arcade top-down co-op shooter in one: the mechanical dinosaur you snap off the sprue and paint at the bench is the unit you then fight with against waves of wind-up toys.
interpretation: The void mixes action, casual, relaxing, simulation, strategy, top-down, arcade, PvE and online co-op, and it is strongly anti-narrative: story tags scored very negative. Its neighbours include diorama, model-kit and shmup games. So the idea is a game with almost no story that joins a calm building sim to a co-op arena shooter.

title: Bean to Cup
short_description: Roll, bounce and race as a single coffee bean across an open fantasy storybook world, from mountain farm to steaming cup. A colorful third-person physics adventure that quietly teaches how real coffee is grown and brewed.
description:
Every cup of coffee starts as a cherry on a mountainside. This one starts with you: a small, stubborn bean named Arabel who wants to see the world.

Roll through a bright, open 3D fantasy world in third person. Bounce down terraced hills, ride drying racks like slides, tumble through a spinning roaster and slip past grinders that would love to make you powder. The physics are soft and playful, so every fall is a chance to try a new route, and quick reflexes help you dodge hungry birds and rolling barrels.

Each connected region is a step in coffee's real journey: picking, washing, sun-drying, sorting, shipping, roasting and brewing. Friendly farm spirits and a sleepy café cat explain what is happening and why, so you learn more about your morning cup than most baristas ever do.

Wander freely, collect flavor notes hidden off the beaten path, and unlock new bean skins. When you want a challenge, race other players' beans online through bouncy obstacle courses.

Relaxing, colorful and full of little discoveries, it is a big adventure for a very small bean.
pitch: An open-world physics adventure in third person where you play the coffee bean itself, and each region you roll through is a real step from farm to cup, which makes it an educational game without any quiz screens.
interpretation: The void is overwhelmingly Casual (0.88), with light Action, 3D, Colorful, Third Person, Relaxing, Fantasy, Physics, Education and Open World, plus a small Online PvP signal. The parent Coffee Beans and the driving/physics parents suggested coffee plus playful physics. Making the player the bean and turning the coffee process into an open world scored better than coffee trucks or café sims.

title: Starfall Over Taihoku
short_description: During the air raids of 1945 Taipei, a schoolgirl finds a crashed rocket that is not from this world. An anime sci-fi action RPG that begins in wartime and ends in space.
description: In the last summer of the war, sirens sound over Taipei almost every day. Lin Mei-hua is fourteen, and she has learned to run when the sirens start. One morning, in a crater by the river, she finds a sleek silver rocket that no army built, and a small voice inside it asking for help. Starfall Over Taihoku is a 2D anime action-adventure in two halves. On the ground, you sneak through bombed streets and shelters, gathering parts and keeping the rocket secret while helping neighbors survive the raids. Then the rocket wakes, and the story leaves the earth: pilot it in fast side-scrolling shooter stages through orbit, asteroid belts and the derelict stations of the travelers who lost it. Salvage you bring back levels up the rocket's weapons and shields, while the friends Mei-hua makes along the way unlock new skills and story paths. Every chapter is told through hand-drawn scenes and quiet conversations about family, loss and courage. The goal is to send the stranger home before the war ends, and to decide what Mei-hua will carry back down to earth.
pitch: An anime story-driven action RPG that joins a historical home-front survival story (1945 Taipei under air raids) to a space shooter, as a schoolgirl repairs and flies home an alien rocket she found in a bomb crater.
interpretation: The hole sits between an anime/JRPG/space-shooter cluster and a WWII-Taiwan adventure parent (Raid on Taihoku), with rocket and asteroid parents. Its decoded tags are Action, Adventure, Anime, Sci-fi, Space, RPG, Shooter and Story Rich. Combining the wartime-Taipei and alien-rocket parts got much closer than a pure anime space RPG did.

title: Seeds of Freedom
short_description: A third-person adventure about football, board games and history in a West African village.
description: It is early 1957 and Kofi has come home from the city to his grandfather's village on the Gold Coast, weeks before the country becomes Ghana. The village football club has been invited to play an exhibition match on Independence Day, and Kofi wants a place on the team. In this relaxed third-person 3D adventure you wander the market, the cocoa farms, the mission school and the chief's courtyard, talking to neighbours, running errands and training on the red dirt pitch by the river. Football matches are quick, arcade-style kickabouts that anyone can play. In the evenings the elders gather to play Oware, and beating them at the ancient board game is the only way to earn their stories about the cocoa boom, the colonial schools and the long road to freedom. A short, gentle and educational adventure about a real moment in history, told through sport, games and the people who played them.
pitch: An educational third-person village adventure set on the eve of Ghana's independence, where you earn your place through street football and Oware matches, and winning at the board game unlocks oral history.
interpretation: The neighbours are small regional-culture games (dominoes, a Brazilian city tour, a Polish commune, an African-president sim), and the decoded tags add adventure, historical, sports, board game, education and walking sim. The hole reads as a culturally specific historical walking adventure built around a traditional board game and sport. A Ghana 1957 setting beat Korean, Brazilian and Irish versions by a wide margin.

title: The Silent Score
short_description: A musician who has lost his hearing returns to the island where he wrote his first song. Explore its silent shores, recover the melodies scattered across it, and face the bosses that guard each one in bullet-hell duels set to music.
description: Teo wrote the songs everyone hummed, until the day he could no longer hear them. He returns to the island where he grew up and finds it silent. Explore the colourful island in top-down 2D, from tide pools and lighthouse cliffs to the overgrown concert hall at its heart. Each region hides a fragment of a lost song, and each fragment is guarded by a creature born of Teo's memories: an old teacher, a rival, a love he left behind. Dodge, dash and strike back in time with the music. Learn to dodge by seeing the beat before you can hear it. Recover a song and colour floods back into that part of the island in bright, psychedelic waves. The soundtrack grows richer with every melody you recover. A short, emotional action-adventure about grief, art and learning to listen again.
pitch: An emotional top-down exploration game with bullet-hell boss duels whose patterns follow music the deaf hero cannot hear, so the player learns to read rhythm visually while each recovered song brings colour and sound back to the island.
interpretation: A gap between a music and rhythm adventure (Beatbuddy), an emotional island-exploration story (Innocence Island), psychedelic bullet hell and boss-centred emotional action. The decoded tags (2D action-adventure, atmospheric exploration, colourful, bullet hell, emotional, story rich) and the music and soundtrack tags that probed strongly pointed to an emotional musical journey whose bosses are bullet-hell set pieces.

title: Flyswatter Night Watch
short_description: A small, strange 3D game about a sleepy night watchman in a tiny house full of cute little monsters. Swat them with a flyswatter, collect coins, then nap while the house keeps working.
description:
You are the night watchman of a very small, very odd house. Every night, cute little monsters crawl out of the walls: round ghosts, fuzzy spiders, giant mosquitoes, sock goblins. They are not really dangerous, just annoying.

Walk the dim 3D rooms in first person, swat monsters with your trusty flyswatter, and collect the coins they drop. Spend coins on silly upgrades like a bigger swatter, a louder alarm clock, or a cat that hunts while you sleep.

When you get tired, go to bed. The house keeps working without you, and when you wake up there are new coins, new rooms, and sometimes a new monster waiting at the foot of the bed.

Simple controls, short sessions, a little action, soft low-poly visuals with a slightly creepy touch. Relaxing, cute and a little spooky. Suitable for all ages. Play for five minutes or leave it running all day.
pitch: A first-person cute-horror idle game: you actively swat harmless little monsters around a tiny house, then go to sleep and let the house, your traps and your cat keep earning for you.
interpretation: This hole sits among a weird casual medieval FPS, bug-swatting jokes (Bug Off, mosquito), a child's-nightmare roguelite and an idle desktop companion. The decoded tags (Casual, 3D, Horror, Cute, Idler, First-Person, Relaxing, Minimalist) suggest a small, slightly spooky first-person game you can leave running.

title: Masha's Icy Way Home
short_description: Walk a little girl home from school across a small Siberian town in the winter of 2003. Slip, slide and score your way down frozen sidewalks in a cute pixel arcade game, and notice how the town changes a little more every evening.
description:
Every evening Masha walks home from school along the same frozen street: past the bakery, the bus stop, the playground and the long grey apartment blocks. The sidewalk is pure ice, and getting home in one piece is a game.

Each walk is a short arcade run. Shuffle, slide and balance across the ice, hop over puddles and snowbanks, grab coins for sweets at the kiosk and chain near-misses for a higher score. The pixel art is bright and cozy, the music is cheerful, and the cats on the stairwell are very cute. Some evenings she gets home safe and warm; some evenings she takes a tumble and has to get up again.

But the walk home is never quite the same. A streetlight that was not there yesterday. A neighbour who waves from a window of an empty building. A song on the radio that knows her name. As the days pass, the town quietly rearranges itself, and the shortest way home starts leading somewhere else. A cozy retro arcade game with a slow, creeping psychological horror story hidden in the snow.
pitch: A cute score-attack arcade game about slipping across icy sidewalks, played as a child's daily walk home in a 2003 Siberian town, where the route itself slowly becomes a psychological horror story.
interpretation: The hole sits between the 2000s psychological horror games Moonchild and Kindawn (set in Yakutia), the arcade game Slippery Sammy (slipping on icy sidewalks) and cute, cozy pixel games. The decoded tags are Cute, Casual, Pixel Graphics, Psychological Horror and Arcade. Naming a Siberian town in the early 2000s gave the biggest gain.

title: The Hill Remembers
short_description: A psychological horror platformer about a child's red ball rolling down the endless hill of a town emptied by a catastrophe. Bounce and steer through ash-grey streets, and find out who keeps carrying you back to the top.
description: The Hill Remembers is an atmospheric 3D physics platformer about a red rubber ball that cannot stop rolling. The town on the hill was emptied in a single night when the sky turned grey, and every street leads down. Steer through yards, staircases, playgrounds and flooded basements, bounce off cars and fences, and use slopes and ramps to clear gaps and reach hidden paths. It begins almost cozy, the sun low and the streets quiet, but each time you reach the bottom, something carries you back to the top, and the town has changed. Doors are open that were closed. Toys have moved. A shape stands in the window of the house at the end of the road. The horror is psychological and slow, built from repetition, silence and small wrong details in a stylized, soft world. Runs are short and linear, controls are just steering and a bounce, and the story is told entirely through what you roll past.
pitch: A cozy roll-down-the-hill physics toy that turns into a looping psychological horror story: each time you roll down, the post-apocalyptic town at the bottom has changed in small, wrong ways.
interpretation: This hole sits between the cozy physics toy 'Roll it down the hill!', horror and post-apocalyptic cinematic platformers (Becloudead, SCP: Submerged, All Hallows) and a narrative object-platformer (DRIFTED). A rolling object in an emptied, slowly changing town covers all of them; a drifting-bag version came too close to DRIFTED.

title: The Last Löyly
short_description: A surreal first-person shooter in a sauna at the end of the world. Keep the stove burning, throw steam at the cold, and shoot back the frost that crawls out of the endless night.
description:
The Last Löyly is a surreal, psychedelic first-person VR shooter set in a Finnish sauna at the end of the world. One morning the sun did not rise. The lake froze to the bottom, the forest turned to glass, and the sauna on the shore became the only warm place left.

Between attacks you run the sauna as a realistic physics simulation. Split logs, feed the stove, carry water from the ice hole and keep the stones hot. Every ladle of water on the stones releases a wave of steam that heals you and pushes the cold back.

Then the frost comes to life. Ice figures, frozen elk and whispering shapes crawl over the snow toward the light. Hold them off with an old hunting shotgun, a flare pistol and buckets of boiling water, aiming by hand in VR or with a mouse on a flat screen.

Stay in the heat too long and the steam brings psychedelic visions of the summer that is gone. Survive the long night and find out why the sun went out.
pitch: A first-person survival shooter where the base you defend is a working sauna sim: heat the stones, throw steam to heal and push back the cold, and shoot living frost at the end of the world, with psychedelic steam visions.
interpretation: This hole sits right beside Saunageddon, a sauna investigation comedy, inside a ring of first-person VR, realistic-sim, psychedelic and shooter games. The decoded tags are First-Person, Action, Simulation, Shooter, Atmospheric, VR and Realistic. So the gap is a sauna game that is an atmospheric VR shooter and simulation rather than a dialogue-led investigation.

title: Supper at the River of Night
short_description: Cook the last meal for every soul crossing into the afterlife. Draw ingredient cards, listen to the stories of the newly dead, meet the underworld's quotas, and serve the dish that decides where they go next.
description:
At the edge of the River of Night stands a small, crooked inn, and every soul must eat there before crossing. You are its new cook, bound to the stove by a contract you do not remember signing, and the underworld's management expects results.

Each night a handful of guests arrive: a greedy merchant, a knight who died of embarrassment, a witch who insists she is only visiting. Talk with them in short visual novel scenes, learn what they regret and what they loved, then draw ingredient cards from a pantry stocked with memories, spices and strange things from the river.

Service is short and tense. Combine cards into dishes before the candles burn down and the ferryman's bell rings. A meal that matches a soul's story sends them gently onward; a careless one sends them somewhere much worse. Between nights, plan the week turn by turn, balancing a shrinking pantry, the inn's debts and the quarterly soul quotas set by a very polite demon accountant.

Unlock darker recipes, upgrade the kitchen and uncover how you ended up here. Grim, funny and quietly moving, every ending is cooked by your hand.
pitch: A card-based cooking game where each dish is a judgment: you learn a dead soul's story in visual-novel scenes and then build the final meal that decides where they go, while an underworld bureaucracy sets quotas you have to meet.
interpretation: The decoded tags combine strategy, cards and visual-novel storytelling with dark fantasy, dark humor, cooking and time management. Among the parents and neighbours are an end-of-the-universe restaurant, a satire of capitalism (Zantar) and an underworld eatery. I read this as a gap for a grim, funny afterlife inn where the cooking, played with cards, carries the narrative choices.

title: Kit of Cornertown
short_description: A desktop companion who lives on your screen and runs missions in her own tiny shooter city while you work. Click to send her out, buy her new cars, and talk to her: she remembers what you said.
description: Kit lives in a tiny city in the corner of your screen, and she is the only hero it has. She talks to you between missions, remembers what you said last week, and writes you a letter when you are away. When the clockwork gangs raid the town, she heads out on missions, and you can watch her run and shoot through the streets in tiny firefights full of bullets and gold. When you want a break, click to take control and play a mission yourself. Every mission pays out in coins for new cars, weapons, clothes and furniture, and the town slowly comes back to life as shops reopen and neighbors return. Off duty she sleeps, cooks and tinkers with her car while you work, study or browse. How you treat her, and which jobs you send her on, decide which of several endings her story reaches, from settling down as the town mechanic to setting off to find where the clockwork gangs come from. Built to run lightly in the background, it is a companion first and a shooter whenever you want one.
pitch: A desktop companion who has her own little third-person shooter world: she idles through missions in a tiny city while you work, remembers your conversations, and you can take over any mission yourself, with several life-sim endings.
interpretation: The hole lies between a remembering, letter-writing desktop-companion parent and open-world money-and-cars shooter parents, with Idler, Life Sim, Multiple Endings and Shooter decoded. The game is a companion whose idle life is a playable mission-based shooter.

title: The Long Patrol
short_description: A 1988 Vietnam veteran relives the war in his nightmares, one card at a time. A retro pixel-art horror deckbuilder.
description: Ohio, 1988. Every night, Frank Doyle is back in Vietnam, and the jungle has changed: radio static that speaks his name, a patrol that never ends, shapes in the elephant grass that are not quite soldiers. In this retro pixel-art roguelite deckbuilder you fight through Frank's nightmares one night at a time. Command your old squad as a hand of cards: point man, radio operator, medic and machine gunner, each with their own deck. Battles play like a tiny tactical wargame: position your squad, call in support and hold the line until dawn. Fear is a resource: let it climb too high and your squad starts to break. By day, the waking world is a small life of its own: the veterans' hall, a phone call to your daughter, a late movie on cable, and each choice reshapes the deck you will take back into the dark. Survive thirty nights, piece together what really happened on that last patrol, and decide what Frank needs to let go of.
pitch: A retro roguelite card battler set inside a Vietnam veteran's recurring nightmares in 1988, where your old squad is your hand of cards and each night plays out as a small tactical wargame.
interpretation: The parents mix a nightmare deckbuilder (Joey's Nightmare II), 1980s Vietnam wargames (Conflict in Vietnam, Men of War: Vietnam), and horror titles (CAMERAMAN NEVER DIES, Opioid visions 88). The decoded tags (strategy, card battler, pixel, horror, 1980s/1990s, turn-based, deckbuilding) fit a veteran's war nightmares as a retro horror deckbuilder. Cameraman-shoot and 80s-suburb takes scored lower.

title: Rewind at Gallows Gulch
short_description: A cowardly sheriff and his overconfident deputy chase monsters through a cursed western town, rewinding time to undo their mistakes. A grid-based comedy horror puzzle platformer for one or two players.
description: Tonight the saloon is full of ghouls, the bank vault is haunted, and the only lawmen left are a sheriff who is afraid of the dark and a deputy who is afraid of nothing and should be. Each level is a cartoony 2D puzzle platformer stage packed with traps, monsters and very bad ideas. Every step on the grid counts, because the monsters only move when you do. Plan your moves, think before you jump and work together: one lawman lures a creature while the other sneaks past. When it all goes wrong, and it will, pull out the sheriff's cursed pocket watch and rewind time a few moves to try again. Solve puzzles, capture each monster alive and lock it up in the town jail, where the prisoners start offering unhelpful advice. Play alone by switching between the two, or team up with a friend in online co-op for twice the chaos. Swing on chandeliers, ride runaway mine carts and push coffins onto pressure plates across haunted saloons, flooded mines and a graveyard that will not stay quiet.
pitch: A turn-based, grid-based 2D puzzle platformer and comedy horror western for two lawmen: monsters move only when you move, and a cursed pocket watch rewinds bad plans, playable solo or in online co-op.
interpretation: The hole sits between turn-based convict tactics (Convict Team Tactics), a casual time-rewind co-op puzzle platformer (Plane Ranger), a sheriff survival platformer, Lovecraftian co-op cards and a nightmare puzzle platformer. The decoded tags (adventure, puzzle, 2D platformer, comedy, strategy, cartoony, horror, co-op) and tactics-flavoured tag probes led to a two-hero comedy horror puzzle platformer. Making it grid-based and turn-based, with rewind as undo, pushed it to 0.85.

title: Pip and the Wandering Wonder Circus
short_description: A colorful 2D puzzle RPG about a traveling circus of misfit mages. Roll a magic ball through puzzle rooms to gather colored stars, battle monsters in quick action fights, and put on shows to bring wonder back to a gloomy, haunted kingdom.
description:
Ever since the Grey Duke banned laughter, the towns of Pelloria have gone quiet, colorless and a little bit eerie. Then a creaky wagon rolls into the capital: the Wandering Wonder Circus, a small troupe of misfit mages led by Pip, a young juggler whose enchanted ball can grow, shrink and glow. Behind the painted smiles, every member of the troupe is hiding a sad secret.

Travel from town to town, explore candlelit forests, flooded mines and a gloomy gothic castle, and help the locals with their problems. Every area is full of puzzle rooms: roll the ball through mazes so it pulls in matching colored stars and leaves the cursed ones behind, bounce it off mirrors and bumpers, and use each performer's magic to reach new places. Monsters lurking along the road are fought in short, snappy action battles where you swap between party members on the fly.

In every town, put on a show. Pick acts, arrange the stage and time your spells to bring color back to the streets and recruit new friends to the troupe.

A warm, funny story about friendship, with bright anime-style art and plenty of secrets to find.
pitch: A story-rich 2D JRPG where the party is a traveling circus. Exploration is ball-physics puzzles built around the juggler's enchanted ball, and each town's arc ends in a staged magic show that wins it back.
interpretation: This hole lies between a circus ball puzzle-platformer, a ball that attracts colored cubes, a castle-cleaning physics puzzle, a gothic RPG Maker horror and a rhythm JRPG. The decoded tags (2D, RPG, Casual, Puzzle, JRPG, Colorful, Fantasy, Story Rich) pointed to a colorful puzzle JRPG with a faintly eerie, circus-and-ball identity.

title: Cartridge Cartel '91
short_description: Run a game company in the 1990s console wars. Design cartridges, rig the arcades, steal rivals' mascots and squeeze players for every coin, in a satirical PvP business sim for up to four friends, in VR or on screen, or team up in co-op to survive the crash.
description:
It is 1991, home consoles are exploding and four tiny studios want to rule the shelves. Each player runs one of them, on a monitor or from a cramped virtual office in VR. Hire developers, pick genres from fighting games to flight sims, gamble on the coming virtual reality craze, build cartridges in a simple drag-and-drop design screen, and then actually play your own games in short arcade tests to see if they are any good.

The real competition is dirty. Bribe magazine reviewers, sabotage a rival's launch party, copy their hit with a cheaper knockoff, and invent ever more outrageous ways to make players pay: secret codes sold by phone, collectible cartridges, exclusive colour variants. At every trade show, rival bosses settle scores in head-to-head arcade duels using each other's games. Each season the market reacts, and greedy decisions can backfire spectacularly.

Play competitive PvP matches online or on the same screen, or join forces in co-op campaigns against ruthless AI publishers. Loud, funny and painfully familiar, it is a business simulation about how video games learned to sell themselves.
pitch: A satirical multiplayer business sim of the 1990s console wars in which you actually play the arcade games your studio ships, settle rivalries in head-to-head duels, and can run your studio from a VR office.
interpretation: The strongest parents are a PvP/co-op exorcism game (Vade Retro), a satire of pay-to-win monetisation (Pay2Win) and a retro console collection (Videopac). The decoded tags are Simulation, Action, PvP, Co-op, VR, Retro, Comedy, Arcade and 1990's. I read the gap as a competitive comedy sim about how 90s games learned to monetise. The exorcism reading drifted toward adult-tagged neighbours, so I dropped it, and VR support gave a clear gain.

title: Nora Off the Page
short_description: Run through the pages of a talking pop-up book. Each chapter is read aloud and fully animated, then turns into a fast, cute runner as Nora races to catch the little aliens escaping from her bedtime story.
description: Nora Off the Page is a colorful story adventure for families. Nora's favorite pop-up book is about a crew of tiny aliens, and tonight they have decided to leave it. With every alien that escapes, the story falls apart. Each chapter starts like a voiced storybook, with animated 3D pages, words that light up as they are read and simple choices about what Nora says and where she looks next. Then the chase begins and the game becomes a bright arcade runner. Sprint across paper meadows, cardboard rooftops and the inside of a birthday cake, jump over puddles of spilled ink, slide under fences and collect stars while the runaway aliens zip ahead in their tiny saucers. Catch them and they return to the page, adding new scenes, songs and jokes to the story. Chapters are short and linear, controls are just jump and slide, and a gentle mode keeps younger players going. Funny, warm and quick, it is a story you can read and run.
pitch: A voiced, read-along pop-up storybook where each chapter turns into a cute arcade runner, chasing the runaway aliens back onto the page to rebuild the story.
interpretation: The parents are roughly equal shares of a children's read-along storybook visual novel (Maggie's Farmyard Adventure), an arcade shooter (MINUS ZERO) and a cute female-led alien-food runner (Galactic Gluttony). I joined them as a voiced storybook visual novel with runner chapters about escaping aliens, and kept away from Galactic Gluttony's agent-eats-food premise.

title: Thirteen Doors
short_description: A point-and-click boss rush in a cursed castle. Click to slash, click to dodge, and solve each locked room before the candle burns out, with nothing but a sword and a mouse.
description:
Thirteen Doors is a 2D point-and-click action adventure set in a hand-painted castle that rebuilds itself every night. You are a squire locked inside at sunset, and the only way out is through thirteen doors, each guarded by a boss.

Every room works twice. First it is an escape room: search the painted walls, combine objects and crack the lock. Then the guardian wakes and the room becomes an arena. Click where you want to strike, drag to block, flick to dodge, and weave through bullet-hell patterns of fire, arrows and cursed coins.

A candle burns on the castle clock. Time spent puzzling is time the bosses grow stronger, so you decide when to explore and when to rush. Between rooms you upgrade your sword, armour and charms in a simple RPG screen.

Short runs, hand-drawn bosses who grumble, gloat and sulk when they lose, and the old-school feel of a browser classic, rebuilt for today.
pitch: Each room of a cursed castle is first an escape-room puzzle and then a mouse-only, bullet-hell boss fight, with a burning candle forcing you to trade puzzle time against how strong the next boss gets.
interpretation: The decoded tags are Action, Adventure, 2D, Point & Click, Action RPG, Hack and Slash, Bullet Hell and Time Management. The parents are a Flash point-and-click hack-and-slash RPG, a castle-basement shop and an escape-room castle. Probes favoured Boss Rush and Escape Room. So the gap is a castle where point-and-click puzzles and click-driven boss fights share every room.

title: Loaded Die
short_description: You are a die. Every time you tumble, the face that lands on top changes how you jump, dash and fight. Roll through brutal pixel-art platforming runs, solo or in couch co-op, where the right number at the right moment is everything.
description:
Somewhere in a forgotten arcade cabinet, a single six-sided die has escaped the board. Now it has to roll, bounce and flip its way through a crumbling world of tiles and traps to get home.

You do not just move, you tumble. Each roll turns the die a quarter turn, and the face that lands on top decides your power: one lets you float, two gives a double jump, three a wall cling, four a ground pound, five a dash, and six a burst of fire. Every screen is a small puzzle: count your rolls so the right face is up before you reach the gap, the spikes or the enemy.

Runs are built from random side-scrolling rooms with bouncy, physics-driven movement, crumbling platforms, conveyor belts, card-soldier enemies and loaded dice that cheat. Between floors you carve new pips onto your faces, swap abilities and gamble on risky upgrades that reshape your whole build.

It is a difficult, arcade-fast platformer with a roguelite heart, plus a casual mode with extra checkpoints. Bring a friend in local co-op as a second die and roll together.
pitch: A precision platformer where how you move is itself the puzzle: whichever face of the die lands on top sets your current ability, so you plan every roll ahead, and a roguelite layer lets you rewrite the faces between floors.
interpretation: The void is a tight 2D pixel-art action platformer with strong Puzzle, Roguelite and Physics signals and some couch co-op. Its parents (Blockdown's grid rolling, Tilebound's tile-built loadouts, HEXED DELTA's geometric shapes, Wood Guy's physics) point to a rolling-block hero whose orientation is the build. The nearest existing game, DICEASTER, uses faces as health. This game uses them as abilities.

title: Rooftop Rations
short_description: A roguelike FPS where you defend your town from invaders and decide how to feed its people, in a world where food is contraband. Fight in first person, then choose who eats and what to build.
description: The Ministry owns every seed and every loaf, and growing your own food is a crime. Yet in a flooded quarter of the old city, a small free town has planted gardens on the rooftops, and you are the one who keeps it alive. Each run you head out in first person to defend the town from Ministry raids and bring home whatever food you can carry. Streets, patrols, weapons and convoys are randomized every time, and the pixel-art firefights are fast and unforgiving. Fall, and the haul is lost. Back home, the shooting stops and the town sim begins. Share out the food, plant the rooftops, build workshops and decide how far to trust the smugglers who want a cut. Feed the gunsmith and your weapons improve, starve the radio crew and you miss the next convoy, turn away refugees and the town remembers. Every choice shapes who follows you and how the Ministry answers. Keep the gardens growing until the city is ready to rise.
pitch: A roguelike first-person shooter tied to a food-rationing town sim: each run's haul from raids decides who in a hidden rooftop-garden town gets fed, and those choices feed back into your weapons, allies and the regime's response.
interpretation: The hole is anchored by a roguelite food city-builder (Feastopia), FPS roguelites, and food-contraband and town-order sims. Its decoded tags are Simulation, Shooter, Strategy, RPG, Roguelike, FPS and Choices Matter. 'Defend your town and decide how to feed its people, where food is contraband' landed closest.

title: Tick of the Gun
short_description: A post-apocalyptic western puzzle roguelike: every gunman shoots when you do. Arrange the chaos so you are the last one standing.
description: Two hundred years after the bombs, the West is wild again, and every meeting ends with guns drawn. Each encounter in this roguelike puzzle game is a frozen standoff on a small isometric grid: raiders, scavengers and rogue robots, each aiming at someone, each with a rule for how they react. Every action you take, a step, a shot, a dive behind a wreck or a kicked fuel barrel, moves the world forward one tick, and every bullet in the air moves with it. Read the lines of fire, predict who will shoot whom, and turn the standoff into a readable bullet hell that ends with you still breathing. Each standoff is a logic puzzle with a clean solution, but the wasteland is procedurally generated and death is permanent. Between encounters, recruit drifters with strange guns and stranger rules, patch up your ride and push further down the highway. Short runs, arcade-quick retries and brutally difficult late fights. Count every bullet and walk away.
pitch: A permadeath wasteland roguelike where every fight is a frozen multi-gunman standoff and bullets advance one tick per action, so a bullet hell becomes a readable logic puzzle you solve to be the last one standing.
interpretation: The decoded tags (strategy, puzzle, action, roguelike, difficult, shooter, bullet hell, turn-based, post-apocalyptic, logic) and parents (One Shot All Kill, Everyone Must Die, Viking Nudgers, 2080 APOCALYPSE) point to turn-based shooting puzzles in a ruined world. Turret-crossfire, falling-wreckage and time-stops bullet-hell takes scored lower than tick-based post-apocalyptic standoffs. The final game deliberately differs from the Everyone Must Die neighbour: here you survive rather than make everyone die, and it adds a roguelike road trip, drifter recruits and visible bullet travel.

title: Recall 1916
short_description: Train your memory and your eyes like a WWI scout: short pattern drills, spot-the-difference maps and memory duels against other players online.
description: This calm, abstract game about war, memory and attention is inspired by real training methods used in the First World War. The battlefield is shown for three seconds, then hidden. Memorize a pattern of trenches, wire and craters on a small pixel-art grid, then rebuild it from memory. Each level is a small battle map drawn in coloured squares. Read a sequence of lamp flashes and repeat it back. Remember where every soldier stood. In VR, the battle map lies on a wooden field table in front of you. Climb the ranks from private to general as your memory improves, and learn about history while training your brain. Challenge other players online in quick memory duels. Simple pixel graphics and a calm soundtrack. No violence, no gore, just focus, patience and a steady eye.
pitch: A non-violent, minimalist memory and attention trainer built on WWI scouting drills: rebuild hidden pixel battle maps, repeat lamp signals and duel other players online, on a flat screen or on a VR field table.
interpretation: The hole sits between an experimental war-memory piece (!Dream), war MMO and wargames, a card game and minimalist memory and visual-acuity puzzles (memory maze, Color Clash, Memory Matrix). The decoded tags (casual, simulation, strategy, minimalist, war, abstract, education, wargame, VR, relaxing) combine into an educational war-themed memory trainer with online PvP duels.

title: Floppy Fault
short_description: A difficult, minimalist retro puzzle platformer with a gun and roguelike runs. Solve one-screen logic puzzles inside a forgotten 1980s home computer, and when you get it wrong, shoot your way through the bullets.
description:
Remember the action puzzle classics of the eighties and early nineties? Simple rules, colored pieces, one screen, and a timer ticking down. You are a tiny hero inside one of those old computers, trying to fix a corrupted floppy disk.

Each screen is a small logic puzzle: push blocks, light switches, connect wires or sort colored pixels into the right slots. Solve it cleanly and the next screen loads. Make a mistake and the glitches fight back, spawning bugs that fill the screen with bullets. Jump between platforms, dodge, shoot back with your little blaster and finish the puzzle under fire.

The disk is different every time you load it, so every run is new. Collect upgrades between screens: an undo charge, a slow-motion shield, a shot that freezes bugs into stepping stones. Lose all your lives and reboot from the start.

Clean minimalist pixel art, chiptune music and short runs. Easy to learn, hard to master, and much harder when you rush.
pitch: A puzzle platformer where mistakes are punished with bullet-hell waves instead of a reset, built into roguelite runs through a corrupted retro floppy disk.
interpretation: This hole sits between an Amiga marble-sorting action-puzzle remake (Logical Now!) and a Sovietpunk roguelite bullet hell (ReLinked), with puzzle platformers nearby.
