The decoded tags (Puzzle, 2D, Retro, Platformer, Action Roguelike, Bullet Hell, Minimalist, Difficult) suggest a retro one-screen puzzle game that turns into a shooter. Sci-fi and space settings pulled the drafts away, so the setting became the inside of an old home computer.

title: Iron Lullaby
short_description: A battered war robot finds an orphaned girl in the ruins of a city it helped destroy. Shoot your way through roguelite twin-stick runs against robot legions each night, and raise her through branching days where every choice changes who she becomes.
description:
The war machines won, then forgot why they were fighting. Unit K-7 is one of them, damaged and alone, until it finds Ilse, eight years old, hiding in the cellar of a bombed school. K-7 decides to keep her alive. It has no idea how.

Nights are roguelite runs. Leave the shelter and blast through procedurally arranged streets in fast twin-stick bullet hell combat against the robot legions that still patrol the city. Collect food, medicine and parts, upgrade your weapons and frame between runs, and get home before dawn. Fail and Ilse goes hungry.

Days play out as a branching visual novel about raising a child. Ration what you scavenged to meet her needs, answer her questions about her parents, decide what to tell her about what you are, and help her cope with nightmares, loneliness and the other survivors who hate machines. Every choice shapes who she becomes and how she sees you, and the story has many endings, not all of them with K-7 in them.
pitch: A war-time parenting drama played from the side of the enemy machine: roguelite twin-stick runs at night pay for the branching choices of the day, and the child grows up shaped by both.
interpretation: The hole lies between My Child Lebensborn (wartime parenting, hatred, resource balancing, choices) and Robot Legions Reborn (twin-stick shooting against robots), with roguelite and visual-novel parents (Flekkia, Bionic Heart 2). The decoded tags are 2D, Choices Matter, Roguelite, CYOA, Visual Novel, Bullet Hell and Robots. Putting the shooter loop first in the text and in the blurb raised the score.

title: Bert's Big Week
short_description: The new mayor of a tiny mountain village has one week before the zombies arrive. Solve silly point-and-click puzzles by day, then click your way through the night defending the town you just about held together.
description: Bert's Big Week is a comedic pixel art adventure with a tower defense twist. Bert won the election in a village of forty people because nobody else ran, and on his first day the radio announces a zombie outbreak heading up the valley. Days play like a classic point-and-click adventure: explore the village, talk to its odd residents, collect strange items and combine them to solve puzzles, from convincing the baker to make cement bread to teaching the goat to guard the gate. Every solved problem becomes something useful for the night: a pie catapult, a scarecrow trap, a volunteer with a frying pan. When the sun sets, the view switches to a top-down map of the village. Place your defenses along the lanes, click on shuffling zombies to bonk them, and spend the coins they drop on quick upgrades while the waves grow sillier and bigger. Survive the week, keep everyone in one piece and uncover where the zombies came from.
pitch: A classic comedy point-and-click adventure where every puzzle you solve by day becomes a defence for that night's clicker tower-defence siege by goofy zombies.
interpretation: The decoded tags are pixel-art 2D point & click comedy adventure (Nelson and the Magic Cauldron, Death Corp) mixed with Strategy, Zombies and Top-Down (Lord Clicker, Before the Snow, Pixel Combat). A day/night split covers both: adventure puzzles by day, clicker tower defence by night. A potion-brewing version and a pure clicker version scored lower.

title: Mallet Marshal
short_description: Command a tiny army with nothing but a mallet. Tap to march, knock twice to charge, and whack the moles and goblins that pop out of the battlefield, one clumsy swing at a time.
description:
Mallet Marshal is a casual VR physics strategy game. A tiny army lives in a field full of holes, and you are the giant with the mallet.

Your soldiers are brave but not very bright. Tap one and it marches where it faces, knock it twice and it charges, knock the ground and the whole squad digs in. Enemy troops march in from the far side, while moles, beetles and burrowing goblins pop up from the holes in between, and every one of them can be whacked too.

The trick is choosing what to hit. Each swing either commands a unit or fights an enemy, never both, so every second is a quick tactical decision. Physics does the rest: soldiers tumble, shields bounce, and a wild swing can send your own captain flying.

Minimalist toy-box visuals, short rounds, a score attack ladder and a two-handed hard mode keep the mallet busy.
pitch: A real-time tactics game in VR where your only input is a clumsy mallet: every swing either gives an order to your tiny soldiers or whacks an enemy popping out of the holes, never both.
interpretation: The hole sits among VR whack-a-mole, minimalist placement-strategy, physics-building and VR tower-defense games. The decoded tags are casual, strategy, simulation, physics, VR, minimalist, tactical and comedy, and probes rewarded Intentionally Awkward Controls and Real Time Tactics. So the gap is a strategy game whose command system is a whack-a-mole mallet.

title: Lunar Pest Roll
short_description: A casual arcade shooter meets an incremental dice game. Roll for your loadout, blast mutant pests across an abandoned moon base for high scores, and bank every lucky streak into upgrades that keep stacking while you are away.
description:
Moon Base Delta was evacuated after the lab's experimental cabbages learned to walk. Somebody has to clean it up, and the contract went to the lowest bidder: you.

Before every run you roll the supply dice. The numbers decide your blaster, your oxygen and the odd perk you get to carry: a six might give you a plasma mop, snake eyes a water pistol and a prayer. Then you jump into a short, fast first-person arcade run through the base's corridors, shooting glowing slugs, sprinting carrots and flying spore pods for combos and credits.

Back at the shuttle, the game becomes an incremental strategy layer. Add faces to your dice, weight the odds, hire robot sweepers and build turrets in cleared sectors. Your automated crew keeps working while you are offline, so every return trip starts with a bigger bank and a deeper base.

Prestige the operation for permanent bonuses, chase records on global score leaderboards, and challenge rivals in quick online PvP races to clear the same wing first.

Goofy, quick and very hard to put down.
pitch: An arcade FPS cleanup job wrapped in an idle/incremental dice economy: dice rolls set your loadout for each run, and each run's earnings let you weight the dice and automate the base, with online PvP races on top.
interpretation: This hole sits next to Moonbase 332, a comedy arcade FPS, combined with the dice/roulette incrementals SIX and Roulette Incremental. Decoded tags: Casual, Arcade, Strategy, Incremental, Shooter, Idler, Score Attack, PvP. So I read it as the missing game that crosses a moon-base arcade shooter with a gambling-style idle progression loop. Moving it off the moon dropped the score sharply.
